specStatements.text: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus (eg uranium or plutonium).
Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. Energy is released by the fission reaction.
All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
Students should be able to draw/interpret diagrams representing nuclear fission and how a chain reaction may occur.
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.

concepts.definition: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, for example a uranium or a plutonium nucleus, into two smaller nuclei. It is a nuclear change, not a chemical one: the nucleus itself breaks apart.
Fission happens to nuclei that are both large and unstable. Uranium and plutonium are the examples the specification gives. A small nucleus, or a large but stable one, does not undergo fission.

Fission that occurs without the nucleus being made to split by anything arriving from outside. Spontaneous fission is rare, so a sample of fissionable fuel left alone does not split apart of its own accord to any appreciable extent.
Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. The neutron is taken into the nucleus rather than bouncing off it, and the nucleus then splits.

The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Both are much smaller than the original nucleus, but neither is a tiny fragment: this is not like alpha decay, where a small particle leaves a nucleus that is almost unchanged.
As well as the two smaller nuclei, a fission emits two or three neutrons. These are free neutrons travelling away from the site of the fission, and they are what makes a chain reaction possible.
A fission also emits gamma rays. These are electromagnetic radiation, emitted along with the two smaller nuclei and the two or three neutrons.
Energy is released by the fission reaction. The energy is not produced by burning the fuel chemically; it is released when the nucleus itself splits.

concepts.term: Kinetic energy of the fission products
concepts.definition: All of the fission products have kinetic energy. The two smaller nuclei and every neutron emitted move away from the fission, so each of them carries kinetic energy, not just the neutrons.

The neutrons released by one fission may go on to be absorbed by other unstable nuclei, causing those nuclei to split and release neutrons of their own. Because each fission can release two or three neutrons, the number of fissions can grow from one generation to the next.
In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled. Controlling it does not mean stopping it: it means holding the rate of fission steady so that the energy released by the reactor is controlled.

A chain reaction in which the number of fissions grows unchecked. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction, so a very large amount of energy is released in a very short time.

In a diagram of fission, a small circle arriving at a large nucleus represents the neutron being absorbed. The large nucleus is then shown splitting into two smaller circles of roughly equal size, with two or three further small circles (neutrons) leaving, and gamma rays shown as wavy arrows.

A chain reaction diagram is drawn in generations. One fission at the top releases neutrons; each neutron that is absorbed by another nucleus produces a further fission in the next row. If every neutron drawn causes a fission, the number of fissions per row multiplies from one row to the next.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. Fusion is the opposite kind of change from fission: fission splits one large nucleus, fusion joins two light ones.

concepts.term: Mass converted into the energy of radiation
concepts.definition: In fusion, some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation. The heavier nucleus that forms therefore has slightly less mass than the two light nuclei that joined together.

misconceptions.question: When a uranium nucleus undergoes fission, what does it split into?
misconceptions.correct: Two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, plus two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
misconceptions.misconception: Splitting the nucleus means it comes apart into all its separate protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the nucleus as a bag of loose particles, so 'splitting' suggests the bag bursting and spilling every particle out.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Those pieces are still nuclei, each holding many protons and neutrons together. Only two or three individual neutrons are emitted.

misconceptions.question: Can any nucleus undergo fission if it is hit hard enough?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.
misconceptions.misconception: Any nucleus can be split, so a small nucleus such as helium or carbon can undergo fission too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'splitting the atom' is used loosely in everyday language, so students assume it applies to atoms in general rather than to particular nuclei.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, with uranium and plutonium as the examples. A small nucleus is not a fission fuel, and neither is a large nucleus that is stable.

misconceptions.question: A block of uranium is sitting in a store. Are its nuclei splitting all the time?
misconceptions.correct: Hardly at all. Spontaneous fission is rare; usually the nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission is going on constantly inside the fuel, because unstable nuclei break up on their own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over what they learned about radioactive decay, which does happen spontaneously and at random, and assume fission behaves the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. That is why fission fuel can be stored safely and why a reactor needs neutrons present to keep the reaction going.

misconceptions.question: How does a neutron make an unstable nucleus split?
misconceptions.correct: The nucleus absorbs the neutron, and the nucleus then splits.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus is smashed apart by being struck hard, so any fast particle, such as an electron, would do the job.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The snooker-ball picture of collisions is a powerful one, and diagrams showing an arrow hitting a nucleus look like an impact rather than a capture.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. The neutron is taken into the nucleus, not bounced off it, and it is a neutron specifically, not an electron or a gamma ray.

misconceptions.question: How big are the two nuclei produced by a fission compared with each other?
misconceptions.correct: They are roughly equal in size.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission chips a small piece off the nucleus, leaving one large nucleus and one very small fragment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet alpha decay first, where a small alpha particle leaves a nucleus that is almost unchanged, and they map that picture straight onto fission.
misconceptions.correction: In fission the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Both products are much smaller than the original nucleus. Alpha decay is a different process and is not fission.

misconceptions.question: What radiation is emitted at the moment of fission?
misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays, along with two or three neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission emits alpha and beta particles, because that is what radioactive substances give out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alpha, beta and gamma are learned together as 'the three radiations', so students reach for the whole set whenever a nucleus changes.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific about fission: two or three neutrons plus gamma rays are emitted. Alpha and beta emission belong to radioactive decay, which is a different nuclear change.

misconceptions.question: Apart from the two smaller nuclei, is anything other than neutrons emitted in fission?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Gamma rays are emitted as well as two or three neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission just throws out neutrons; there is no radiation given off at the moment it splits.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chain reaction diagrams draw the neutrons prominently because they are what continues the reaction, and often leave the gamma rays out altogether.
misconceptions.correction: A fission emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. The gamma rays are part of what is emitted at the moment of the split, even when a simplified diagram does not show them.

misconceptions.question: Are the two nuclei produced by a fission identical to each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are roughly equal in size, not necessarily the same.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus splits exactly in half, so the two nuclei produced must be identical.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Splitting' suggests cutting something down the middle, and 'roughly equal' is read as a polite way of saying 'equal'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size. 'Roughly' is doing real work here: the split is not an exact halving and the two products need not be the same.

misconceptions.question: Which of the fission products have kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: All of them: the two smaller nuclei and every neutron emitted.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the neutrons move, so only the neutrons carry kinetic energy away from the fission.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams draw arrows on the neutrons because those are the particles that go on to cause further fissions, so the two nuclei look as though they stay put.
misconceptions.correction: All of the fission products have kinetic energy. The two smaller nuclei recoil from each other and move away, and the emitted neutrons move too, so every product is carrying kinetic energy.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy released in a nuclear power station come from?
misconceptions.correct: It is released by the fission reaction when nuclei split.
misconceptions.misconception: The uranium fuel is burned, like coal in a coal-fired station, and burning it releases the energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'fuel' and the phrase 'burnt-up fuel rods' come from everyday and industrial language, and the rest of the power station really does behave like a conventional one.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is released by the fission reaction itself, when a large unstable nucleus splits. No chemical burning is involved; that is why so much energy comes from so little fuel.

misconceptions.question: Does every neutron released by a fission cause another fission?
misconceptions.correct: No. The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction, but they do not all cause a fission.
misconceptions.misconception: Each neutron released must be absorbed by another nucleus, so every fission automatically triggers two or three more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook chain reaction diagrams show every neutron finding a nucleus, because that is the tidiest way to draw the idea of growth.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. A neutron can escape from the fuel or be absorbed without causing a fission, which is exactly what makes it possible to control the reaction.

misconceptions.question: Are fission and fusion two words for the same nuclear process?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fission splits a large unstable nucleus; fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier one.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission and fusion both mean getting energy out of nuclei, so the two words can be used interchangeably.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words look and sound alike, both appear in the same chapter, and both are described as releasing energy from the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: They are opposite kinds of change. Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus such as uranium or plutonium. Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say the chain reaction in a reactor is controlled?
misconceptions.correct: The reaction is kept going at a steady rate so that the energy released is controlled.
misconceptions.misconception: Controlling the chain reaction means preventing it, so that no chain reaction takes place in a reactor at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Control' is often heard as 'restrain' or 'shut down', and safety language around reactors reinforces that reading.
misconceptions.correction: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The reaction continues; what is controlled is its rate, and therefore the rate at which energy is released.

misconceptions.question: What makes a nuclear weapon explode rather than release energy steadily?
misconceptions.correct: The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: A weapon explodes because it uses a completely different and far more powerful kind of fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a dramatic difference in outcome to come from a dramatic difference in material, rather than from how the same reaction is managed.
misconceptions.correction: The difference the specification draws is control. In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled to control the energy released; in a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled, so the energy is released all at once.

misconceptions.question: In a chain reaction diagram, how does the number of fissions change from one row to the next?
misconceptions.correct: It multiplies, because each fission can release two or three neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Each fission leads to just one more fission, so the same number of fissions happens in every row.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of a chain as a line of single links, one after another, which suggests one event leading to one more.
misconceptions.correction: Read the diagram from the neutrons. One fission emits two or three neutrons, and each neutron that is absorbed causes a further fission, so the number of fissions per row multiplies rather than staying the same.

misconceptions.question: In a chain reaction diagram, are the neutrons drawn in a row the same thing as the fissions in that row?
misconceptions.correct: No. The neutrons leaving one row are absorbed to cause the fissions of the next row.
misconceptions.misconception: Every small circle in the diagram is one fission, so counting the neutrons in a row gives the number of fissions in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both neutrons and fissions are drawn as small repeated symbols, and students count symbols rather than tracking what each one stands for.
misconceptions.correction: Label the diagram as you read it. A fission is a nucleus splitting; the neutrons it emits then travel on and cause the fissions of the following row, so a row of four neutrons produces up to four fissions, not four more neutrons.

misconceptions.question: Which nuclei join together in nuclear fusion?
misconceptions.correct: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion joins two heavy nuclei, because you need big nuclei to get a lot of energy out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate large nuclei with nuclear energy because uranium is the example they meet first, and carry that association into fusion.
misconceptions.correction: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. It is the light nuclei that fuse; heavy unstable nuclei are what undergo fission.

misconceptions.question: How does the mass of the nucleus formed in fusion compare with the two nuclei that joined?
misconceptions.correct: It is slightly less, because some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: The masses simply add up, because mass is always conserved in any change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is taught firmly for chemical reactions and for everyday physical changes, and students apply it to nuclear changes without exception.
misconceptions.correction: In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus has slightly less mass than the total of the two light nuclei. This is a nuclear change, and it is where the energy of the radiation comes from.

misconceptions.question: Two light nuclei have to be pushed together very forcefully to fuse. Does that make the new nucleus heavier than the two put together?
misconceptions.correct: No. The new nucleus has slightly less mass, as some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy had to be supplied to force the nuclei together, so that energy is stored in the new nucleus and makes it heavier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that anything put into a process must show up inside the product, and mass is the only property of the product they can point to.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion releases energy overall: some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus formed has slightly less mass than the two light nuclei that joined together.

options.text: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as a uranium nucleus.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.

options.text: The joining of two light nuclei together to form a single heavier nucleus.
options.rationale: This is the definition of fusion. Students who treat the two similar-sounding words as interchangeable pick whichever they read last.

options.text: The breaking up of a nucleus into all of its separate protons and neutrons.
options.rationale: Students who picture the nucleus as a loose bag of particles read 'splitting' as the whole bag coming apart, rather than as a split into two smaller nuclei.

options.text: The splitting of a small and stable nucleus, such as a carbon nucleus.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think 'splitting the atom' applies to atoms in general and have not registered that the nucleus must be large and unstable.

mcqs.stem: An engineer needs a fuel whose nuclei can undergo fission. Which choice is suitable, and for the right reason?

options.text: Helium, because its nucleus is small and very stable.
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe any nucleus can be split, and who think a small nucleus should be the easiest to break.

options.text: Plutonium, because its nucleus is large and unstable.
options.rationale: Plutonium is one of the two examples the specification gives, and it meets both conditions: the nucleus is large and it is unstable.

options.text: Hydrogen, because its nucleus is the lightest of all.
options.rationale: Hydrogen is associated with nuclear energy through fusion; students who blur fission and fusion offer the lightest nucleus as a fission fuel.

options.text: Lead, because its nucleus is large and does not decay.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember 'large' but not 'unstable', so they select a heavy nucleus that is in fact stable.

mcqs.stem: Usually, for fission to occur, what must happen to the unstable nucleus first?

options.text: It must be struck by a fast-moving electron.
options.rationale: Students holding the snooker-ball picture think any fast particle could knock the nucleus apart, and electrons are the fast particles they know best.

options.text: Nothing: it will shortly split all on its own.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who transfer spontaneous radioactive decay onto fission and forget that spontaneous fission is rare.

options.text: It must first absorb a neutron that hits it.
options.rationale: The specification states that usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.

options.text: It must absorb a gamma ray from another atom.
options.rationale: Gamma rays are emitted by fission, so students reverse the sequence and treat gamma radiation as the trigger rather than a product.

mcqs.stem: A sealed sample of uranium is stored on a shelf. Over many years only a very small number of its nuclei split. Why?

options.text: Fission is happening constantly, but far too slowly to detect.
options.rationale: Students who believe unstable nuclei are always splitting explain the lack of an effect by rate rather than by the rarity of spontaneous fission.

options.text: Uranium nuclei are stable, so they can never undergo fission.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who confuse 'not splitting at the moment' with being stable, and who have lost the condition that fission nuclei are unstable.

options.text: Neutrons cannot be absorbed unless the sample is heated first.
options.rationale: Students who think of the neutron as needing to smash the nucleus assume extra energy must be supplied before anything can happen.

options.text: Spontaneous fission is rare, so almost no nuclei split unaided.
options.rationale: Fission usually requires the nucleus to absorb a neutron first; without that, only the rare spontaneous fissions occur.

mcqs.stem: As well as two smaller nuclei, what does a fission reaction emit?

options.text: Two or three neutrons, plus gamma rays.
options.rationale: The specification states that the nucleus emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.

options.text: Two or three neutrons, and nothing else.
options.rationale: Chain reaction diagrams usually show only the neutrons, so students forget that gamma rays are emitted as well.

options.text: One neutron only, plus alpha particles.
options.rationale: Students who assume nuclear changes give out alpha, beta and gamma reach for alpha, and a single neutron fits their one-in-one-out picture of a chain.

options.text: Two or three protons, plus gamma rays.
options.rationale: A slip between the two nucleons: students recall the number and the gamma rays correctly but name the wrong particle.

mcqs.stem: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. What is true of the two nuclei produced?

options.text: One is almost as large as uranium and the other is very small.
options.rationale: This is the alpha decay picture: a small particle leaves behind a nucleus that is almost unchanged. Students map it onto fission.

options.text: They are roughly equal in size, and both smaller than uranium.
options.rationale: The specification states that the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

options.text: They are always exactly identical to each other in every way.
options.rationale: Students read 'roughly equal' as 'equal' and picture the nucleus being cut precisely down the middle.

options.text: They are each larger than uranium, since two nuclei formed.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think that producing two things must mean more matter than before, rather than the same matter divided.

mcqs.stem: Immediately after a fission, in what forms is the released energy carried away?

options.text: As gamma rays only; the products themselves are left at rest.
options.rationale: Students who think of radiation as the only way energy travels overlook the statement that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

options.text: As kinetic energy of the two or three emitted neutrons alone.
options.rationale: Diagrams put the arrows on the neutrons, so students conclude that only the neutrons are moving and carrying energy.

options.text: As kinetic energy of the fission products and as gamma rays.
options.rationale: All of the fission products have kinetic energy, and gamma rays are emitted, so the energy released is carried away in both forms.

options.text: As chemical energy given out as the uranium fuel burns away.
options.rationale: The word 'fuel' invites a burning model, and the rest of a power station does resemble a conventional one.

mcqs.stem: Which of the products of a fission reaction have kinetic energy?

options.text: Only the neutrons, because only they are moving off.
options.rationale: The neutrons are the products students see drawn with arrows, so they assume the nuclei stay where they are.

options.text: Only the two smaller nuclei, not the emitted neutrons.
options.rationale: Students who link kinetic energy to mass assume the massive nuclei carry it and the light neutrons do not.

options.text: Only the lighter of the two nuclei that are produced.
options.rationale: Students holding the alpha decay picture expect a small fragment to fly off while the large one stays put.

options.text: All of them: both nuclei and every neutron emitted.
options.rationale: The specification states plainly that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes how a chain reaction gets going?

options.text: Neutrons released by one fission are absorbed by other nuclei.
options.rationale: The neutrons emitted may go on to start a chain reaction, because absorbing a neutron is what makes another nucleus undergo fission.

options.text: Gamma rays released by one fission split the nuclei around it.
options.rationale: Students who remember gamma rays as the striking output of fission make them the agent that continues the reaction.

options.text: Electrons knocked off the atoms go on to split other nuclei.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think any fast particle can break a nucleus and who reach for the particle they know best.

options.text: Heat released by one fission makes the nearby nuclei split.
options.rationale: Students using a burning model imagine fission spreading the way fire spreads, by heating what is next to it.

mcqs.stem: The specification says the neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. Why 'may' rather than 'will'?

options.text: Each neutron does cause a fission, but only after a long delay.
options.rationale: Students who believe every neutron must find a nucleus explain 'may' as being about timing rather than about whether it happens at all.

options.text: Some neutrons escape or are absorbed without causing a fission.
options.rationale: A chain reaction only continues if emitted neutrons are absorbed by other unstable nuclei; neutrons that escape the fuel do not, which is what makes control possible.

options.text: Only one neutron is ever released, so the reaction cannot spread.
options.rationale: Students with a one-link-at-a-time model of a chain think there are too few neutrons for growth to be possible.

options.text: Neutrons cause fission only if a gamma ray is emitted as well.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat every listed product of fission as a necessary condition for the next fission.

mcqs.stem: In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled. What is the purpose of controlling it?

options.text: To stop the chain reaction from happening at all.
options.rationale: Students read 'controlled' as 'prevented', which would leave a reactor with no source of energy.

options.text: To stop the fuel from emitting any gamma rays.
options.rationale: Students who focus on radiation as the hazard assume control must be aimed at the emissions themselves.

options.text: To control the energy released by the reaction.
options.rationale: The specification states that the chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released.

options.text: To make the fuel split into equal-sized nuclei.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the roughly equal split is something the reactor has to be adjusted to produce.

mcqs.stem: What is the essential difference between a nuclear reactor and a nuclear weapon?

options.text: A weapon uses a fuel a reactor cannot use at all.
options.rationale: Students expect a dramatic difference in outcome to come from a different material rather than from how the reaction is managed.

options.text: In a reactor the chain reaction is stopped entirely.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'controlled' as 'shut down', and who then have no way to explain where a reactor's energy comes from.

options.text: In a weapon each single fission releases more energy.
options.rationale: Students explain a bigger overall effect by scaling up the individual event, rather than by the number of fissions and the time taken.

options.text: In a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled.
options.rationale: The specification attributes the explosion caused by a nuclear weapon to an uncontrolled chain reaction, in contrast with the controlled reaction in a reactor.

mcqs.stem: A diagram of fission shows a large labelled circle for a uranium nucleus, with a small circle arriving at it from the left. What does the small circle represent?

options.text: A neutron being absorbed by the nucleus.
options.rationale: Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron, and that absorption is what the incoming small circle shows.

options.text: An electron being fired at the nucleus.
options.rationale: Students reading the arrow as an impact choose the fast particle they are most familiar with.

options.text: A light nucleus about to fuse with it.
options.rationale: Two circles moving together look like joining, so students who blur fission and fusion read the diagram as fusion.

options.text: A gamma ray heading into the nucleus.
options.rationale: Gamma rays appear in the fission story, so students place one at the start instead of among the products.

mcqs.stem: In a chain reaction diagram, one fission at the top releases two neutrons, and each neutron is absorbed and causes a further fission. How many fissions are shown in the third row?

options.text: 2 fissions
options.rationale: Students who think each fission leads to just one more expect the count to stay at the row 2 value.

options.text: 4 fissions
options.rationale: Row 1 has 1 fission, which releases 2 neutrons and so gives 2 fissions in row 2; those release 4 neutrons, giving 4 fissions in row 3.

options.text: 8 fissions
options.rationale: Students count the 8 neutrons that row 3 releases instead of the 4 fissions that row 3 contains.

options.text: 3 fissions
options.rationale: Students add one per row instead of multiplying, treating the chain as growing by a single step each time.

options.text: The joining of two heavy nuclei to form a lighter nucleus.
options.rationale: Students associate nuclear energy with heavy nuclei such as uranium and carry that association into fusion.

options.text: The splitting of one heavy nucleus into two lighter ones.
options.rationale: This is fission. Students who treat the two words as interchangeable pick the process they know better.

options.text: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of nuclear fusion.

options.text: The joining of two atoms so that their electrons combine.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who place the change in the electrons, as in bonding, rather than in the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. How does the mass of the new nucleus compare with the total mass of the two light nuclei?

options.text: Exactly the same: mass can never be lost or gained in any change.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass is taught firmly for chemical reactions, and students apply it to nuclear changes without exception.

options.text: Slightly more, because energy had to be supplied to force them together.
options.rationale: Students assume anything put into a process must be stored in the product, and mass is the property they can point to.

options.text: Slightly less, because a neutron is given off as the nuclei join up.
options.rationale: Students transfer the fission picture, where neutrons are emitted, onto fusion and explain the missing mass as a lost particle.

options.text: Slightly less: some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
options.rationale: The specification states that in fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the new nucleus is slightly less massive.
